welcome.title: Welcome to PuriCat
welcome.subtitle: A calm, spreadsheet-native home for your databases.
welcome.noRecent: Connections you open will appear here.
welcome.statusNote: PuriCat is being built in phases. Nothing below is simulated.

features.connections: Saved connections with passwords in the system keychain
features.engines: MySQL and PostgreSQL servers and SQLite files, with TLS and read-only sessions that the server or the file handle enforces
features.browse: Explore databases, schemas, tables and views across several servers at once
features.grid: Fast virtualized data grid with sorting, paging and exact server-side values
features.themes: Light and dark themes, English and Thai
features.editing: Excel-style editing with staged changes, plus Smart Paste: previewed INSERT / UPDATE / UPSERT from a spreadsheet, matched on a key
features.sql: SQL editor with completion and formatting, cancellable runs, history, and CSV / JSON / XLSX export
features.ai: AI agent through your own Claude Code CLI (Codex not yet verified): it can look things up when you allow it, and every change waits for your approval
features.backup: Backups by hand and on a schedule, into a folder you choose, and a restore into a new database
features.restore: Restoring over an existing database, and encrypted backups

ai.contextHint: What the AI is told about your database

contextMissingBody.noTab: Open a table or a query tab to give the AI the schema of that database. Without one, it answers from general knowledge only.

ai.contextBody: The names and types of the tables and columns in the active tab's database, and the SQL in the active query tab. Never rows, host names, user names or passwords.
ai.contextOffBody: Nothing about your database is sent. The AI answers from your messages only.

ai.policy1: The AI cannot touch your database: it has no tools here and only writes text.
ai.policy2: SQL it suggests runs only when you open it in a query tab and run it yourself.
ai.policy3: Only schema names and types, and the active query, are shared. Never rows, hosts, user names or passwords.

policyAccess.schema: The AI can look at the structure of the database in front of you: tables, columns, types and keys. It cannot read rows.
policyAccess.data: The AI can look at the structure of the database in front of you and run read-only queries on it.

ai.policyApprove: It cannot change anything by itself. A change is a proposal: you read the SQL and decide, and PuriCat runs it only if you approve.
ai.policyShareRows: What it reads, rows included, is sent to the provider under your own account. Hosts, user names and passwords never are.

none.label: Off

schema.label: Structure

data.label: Structure and rows
data.body: It can also run read-only queries. The rows it reads are sent to the provider: at most 200 per query, in a read-only transaction.

access.noTab: Open a table or a query tab: the tools work on the database of the tab in front.
access.production: The tab in front is a Production connection. Rows the AI reads from it are sent to the provider.
access.codex: Not yet verified with Codex: its tool calls could not be tested on a working account. Claude Code is verified.

smart.semantics: PuriCat matches the rows itself, then runs plain INSERT and UPDATE statements in one transaction. It does not use ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, ON CONFLICT or MERGE, so only the key chosen here decides which row is the same.
smart.semanticsLarge: PuriCat matches the rows itself, then runs plain INSERT and UPDATE statements, {{batch}} rows per transaction. It does not use ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, ON CONFLICT or MERGE, so only the key chosen here decides which row is the same.
smart.stale: The set-up changed. Preview again before running.
smart.rowsShown: Showing the first {{shown}} of {{total}} rows. All of them are checked.

smart.nothing: Nothing to do: no pasted row would be inserted or changed.

smart.problemRows_other: {{count}} rows have a problem and cannot be written as they are.

smart.skipProblems_other: Leave these {{count}} rows out and run the other {{rest}}
smart.onlyProblems: List only the rows with problems
smart.problemsCopied_one: {{count}} row copied, as it was pasted
smart.problemsCopied_other: {{count}} rows copied, as they were pasted

smart.doneSkipped_other: {{count}} rows with problems were left out

smart.leavingOut_other: {{count}} rows have a problem and will be left out: nothing is written for them. The other {{rest}} run in one transaction.

flushAbout.privileges: Reloads accounts and privileges from the grant tables. Needed only after those tables were edited directly. Recent MySQL versions mark this statement as deprecated.
flushAbout.tables: Closes every open table and empties the table cache. It waits for statements that are using those tables, so a busy server may pause for a moment.
flushAbout.logs: Closes and reopens the server's log files, and starts a new binary log file when binary logging is on.
flushAbout.status: Adds this session's status counters to the global ones and resets them to zero.

schema.prodFlushWarning: This runs on a PRODUCTION server.

definitionFrom.server: The server's own statement, from SHOW CREATE.
definitionFrom.file: The text SQLite keeps in the file, followed by the table's indexes and triggers.
definitionFrom.catalogue: Put together by PuriCat from the catalogue — PostgreSQL has no statement for this. Owner, grants, row-level-security policies, storage parameters and inheritance are not included; pg_dump is the authority.

schema.renameEmpty: Type another name to see the statement.

emptyAbout.mysql: Every row of the table is deleted. TRUNCATE commits at once — it cannot be rolled back — and AUTO_INCREMENT starts again from the beginning.
emptyAbout.postgres: Every row of the table is deleted. This cannot be undone. Identity and serial counters keep their values. If another table refers to this one with a foreign key, the server refuses.
emptyAbout.sqlite: Every row of the table is deleted. This cannot be undone. SQLite has no TRUNCATE, so a DELETE runs and the table's triggers fire.

dropAbout.table: The table is deleted from the server with its rows, indexes and triggers. This cannot be undone. If a view or a foreign key depends on it, the server may refuse.
dropAbout.view: Only the view is deleted; the tables it reads keep their rows. If another view depends on it, the server may refuse.
dropAbout.matview: The materialized view and its stored result are deleted; the tables it was made from keep their rows.

schema.closesTab: Its open tab will be closed.
schema.unsavedTable: A tab of this table has unsaved changes. Save or discard them first.
schema.prodTableWarning: This runs on a PRODUCTION server.
schema.viewNameFixed: To give a view another name, use Rename… in its menu.
schema.viewQueryHint: Only the SELECT — CREATE VIEW … AS is written around it.
schema.viewQueryMysql: MySQL keeps its own rewriting of a view's query, with every name spelled out, not the text that was typed. This is that text.
schema.viewQueryPostgres: A table that is not on the search path needs its schema, as in shop.orders.
schema.viewTryHint: Runs the query read-only and shows its first 100 rows.
schema.viewTriedFirst_one: The first row, there are more
schema.viewTriedFirst_other: The first {{count}} rows, there are more
schema.viewTriedOutdated: The query changed since this preview.

schema.viewEditNote: Whatever reads this view keeps working only if its columns stay compatible.

viewEditNoteOn.postgres: PostgreSQL can add columns at the end, but not remove, rename or retype one: it refuses, and the view stays as it is.
viewEditNoteOn.sqlite: SQLite cannot replace a view: it is dropped and created again, both in one transaction.

sessions.noneRunning: Nothing is running. Idle sessions are hidden.
sessions.pick: Select a session to see its whole query and what can be done to it.
sessions.gone: That session is no longer on the server.
sessions.ownHint: This is the session PuriCat used to read this list.
sessions.readOnly: This connection is read-only: sessions are listed, not stopped or ended.
sessions.endHint: Stopping the query keeps the session. Ending it closes the connection, and the server rolls back a transaction it has open.
sessions.idleHint: Nothing is running in it. Ending it closes the connection, and the server rolls back a transaction it has open.
sessions.confirmQuery: Stop what session {{id}} is running? The session stays connected.
sessions.confirmConnection: End session {{id}}? Its client is disconnected, and a transaction it has open is rolled back.
sessions.privilegeMysql: Without the PROCESS privilege an account sees only its own sessions, and may end only those.
sessions.privilegePostgres: Other accounts' queries are hidden, and cannot be stopped, unless this account is a superuser or a member of pg_read_all_stats / pg_signal_backend.

none.hint: The account alone. Grant what it needs later.

users.name: User name
users.hostHint: % is any host; localhost is the server's own machine.
users.statementsEmpty: Give the user a name, and a database if the template needs one, to see the statements.
users.maskNote: What runs is this text with the real password where the mask is.
users.revealNote: The password is shown as it will be written into the statement.
users.wildcardNote: \_ keeps the underscore from matching any character: in a grant, _ and % in a database name are wildcards.
users.pgDefaultNote: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES covers only what {{role}} — the role this connection uses — creates later. Tables made by another role need a grant of their own.
users.pgPublicNote: Nothing is taken away from PUBLIC: on most servers every role may still connect to the other databases. What it can read there depends on their own grants.
users.readOnly: This connection is read-only, so it cannot change accounts. Turn off the read-only session in its settings first.
users.prodWarning: This changes accounts on a PRODUCTION server.
users.keepPassword: Copy the password now. PuriCat does not keep it, and the server stores only a hash of it.
users.passwordAbout: Whatever connects with the old password stops working once it is changed.

dropAbout.mysql: The account and all its privileges are removed from the server. Sessions it has open keep running until they end.
dropAbout.postgres: The role is removed from the server. PostgreSQL refuses while the role owns objects or still holds privileges: run REASSIGN OWNED BY and DROP OWNED BY for it in a query tab of each database first.
